HOW TO READ POWER RATING

Yes — the bigger the number, the stronger the team, within its own competition. It's a single combined score built from two things: how much a team scores relative to the league average (Attack Strength) and how well it defends relative to the league average (Defence Strength), averaged together. A team can be mid-table in points but still show a high Power Rating if its underlying numbers are genuinely strong — that gap is exactly what makes this different from just reading the league table.

Pythagorean Expectation — Lucky vs Unlucky Records

Estimates the record a team should have based purely on goals scored vs conceded — independent of actual results. A team well above its expected points may be riding an unsustainable run; a team well below may be due for better results if their underlying performance continues. Fitted exponent for this season: k = 1.3 (see Module 40 in the notebook for the full methodology).

This looks at what has already happened this season, not what happens next — for a forward-looking forecast using this same Pythagorean model alongside Elo, see Predicted Final Table under Predictive Ratings.

Scout Intelligence

Coverage NoteVolume vs EfficiencyAll Scorers
The scorers, goals, and cards shown in this section reflect exactly the match details and events KHU has made available on their website for each match — currently 19.0% of matches with a recorded goal. This is not a scraping limitation — it's a genuine gap in the source site's own records. As KHU adds more detail to their match pages over time, this section will automatically reflect that on the next scrape — nothing here needs to be rebuilt by hand when their data improves.
WHAT THE TWO CARDS BELOW ACTUALLY MEAN

Volume vs Efficiency Quadrant — "Volume" just means total goals scored, full stop. "Efficiency" means goals scored relative to how many matches that player's team has actually played. Why both matter together: a player with 3 goals from 3 matches is a far more efficient scorer than one with 3 goals from 15 matches, even though the raw goal count looks identical. Plotting both together sorts every scorer into four groups — high in both (the standout scorers), high volume only (scored a lot, but needed more chances to do it), high efficiency only (fewer goals overall, but reliable when given the chance), and below average in both.

Breakout Candidates — this flags players whose goal tally is so far above what's typical in their own competition that it stands out statistically, not just "a bit better than average." Worth a second look precisely because it's rare — but given how small the underlying sample is (see the note above), this means "stands out within the data we actually have," not a guaranteed claim about who the best player really is.

HOW TO READ THIS CHART

Each square shows how closely two team statistics move together across the season — not whether one causes the other. Green means "when one goes up, the other tends to go up too" (e.g. more goals scored usually means more points). Red means they tend to move in opposite directions (e.g. more goals conceded usually means fewer points). The stronger the color, the stronger that relationship. The row and column both labeled "Points" show, at a glance, which statistics actually track with winning — useful for knowing what to prioritize in training, and what's just noise.

Predictive Ratings

Elo ratings processed match-by-match per competition, validated against actual results rather than just displayed at face value.

What is EloRating TrajectoryTop Elo RatingsPredicted Final TableElo vs Pythagorean
WHAT IS ELO, IN PLAIN TERMS

Elo comes from chess. Every team gets one number representing its current strength — but that number only means something compared to other teams, never on its own. After every match, the winner takes points from the loser, and how many depends on who was expected to win. Beat a team you were expected to lose to, and you gain a lot. Beat a team you were expected to crush anyway, and you barely gain anything. That's what makes it useful: it rewards genuine upsets and stops a team padding its rating by repeatedly beating weak sides.

Every team here starts at a neutral 1500 — nobody has history yet, so nobody gets a head start. Ratings then move up or down after each real result, weighted by how big the win was and who was playing at home.

How good is this model, really? Two checks, in plain terms:
• Does it agree with reality? Teams the model rates highly also tend to finish high in the real table — correlation 0.73 out of a possible 1.00 (1.00 would mean perfect agreement, 0 would mean no relationship at all). 0.73 is a real, strong pattern, not a coincidence — but it doesn't hold for every single team.
• Are its win probabilities well-calibrated? Brier score 0.187 (lower is better) vs. 0.191 for simply guessing the league's average home-win rate every time, with no team-specific information at all. The model beats that baseline — genuinely, but modestly, not dramatically. Every team starts a competition at a neutral 1500 rating, so early-season ratings are naturally less reliable than late-season ones.

Predicted Final Table — Elo vs. Pythagorean (two independent forecasts, side by side — projections, not guarantees)

Elo projects forward by simulating each remaining match using the team's current rating. Pythagorean projects forward by assuming each team's current underlying goal-difference rate continues. When both agree (✓), that's a more confident forecast; when they diverge (⚠), it's worth knowing the two models see this team differently — often because Elo has picked up on recent form that goal difference alone hasn't caught up to yet, or vice versa.

This is a forecast of what happens next — for how a team's current record compares to what their goal difference alone would predict for the season so far, see Pythagorean Expectation under Coach Intelligence.
